catalog_quote: p. 52: "... analysis of spoken Jero suggests that stress and tone are not phonemically relevant. The syllable that is based on the root of verbs and deverbatives and on the initial syllable of nouns and other parts of speech is generally more prominent than the other syllables due to an increase of loudness. Loudness is not always concurrent with highest pitch. The stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words is characterised by a distinctive contrast between the phonemes /i/ and /i:/, /e ..." p. 54: "... stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words are also present in the open syllable of polysyllabic verbs that follows the syllable of the negative prefix <a->. Word stress regularly falls on the root following the negative prefix, but the negative prefix can also be stressed. /nokim/ /noki/ ['nokim] [a'noki] 'wepi are' 'wepi are not'" p. 58: "... unstressed final open syllable of polysyllabic words."
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Vowel length is marginally distinctive in Wambule and Jero. Differences in vowel length are generally not distinctive other than in the stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words and a limited number of other related phonological environments. The opposition between the six vowels which partake in the length contrast is generally neutralised in most environments. The length-neutral vowels are /A, I, U/.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: VERBATIM CHECK: the quoted passage ("Vowel length is marginally distinctive in Wambule and Jero. Differences in vowel length are generally not distinctive other than in the stressed open syllable of polysyllabic words.. The length-neutral vowels are /A, I, U/.") is present word for word in, section "Vowels", second paragraph, as stated. The page describes Wambule and Jero jointly and does not say where stress falls, so the compilers summary of that page is accurate. WHY THE READING AND STATUS CHANGE: the deciding statement in Opgenort 2005, A Grammar of Jero (Brill; Google Books id 38pKEAAAQBAJ) is recoverable through the public Google Books GData volumes feed (https://www.google.com/books/…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The author (the only describer of Jero) states that Jero polysyllabic words have a stressed syllable and that the short/long vowel contrast survives only in that stressed syllable when it is open; the page does not say which syllable is stressed. The same author's Wambule notes (sister language, 'initial stressed syllables') suggest initial stress in the Chaurasia (Wambule-Jero) unit, but that is not asserted for Jero in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Length also distinctive in 'a limited number of other related phonological environments' (unspecified); Hyslop's review adds that the /a/ length contrast is unstable per Opgenort 2005.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (polysyllabic words); data are elicited citation forms from the southern Mohanṭār dialect and the northern Āmboṭ dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: All Jero material is by Jean Robert Opgenort and describes the southern dialect of Mohanṭār (Sindhulī district) and the northern dialect of Āmboṭ (Okhalḍhuṅgā district); Opgenort treats Jero and Wambule (wamb1257) as two mutually intelligible dialect groups of one 'Chaurasia' language, so the Wambule stress remarks held under ('initial stressed syllables') are sister-dialect evidence, not Jero statements. The quoted transcription page speaks of 'Wambule and Jero' jointly.
